text: PCP is: • intravenous or oral co-trimoxazole1-4 Alternative regimens are:1-4 • intravenous pentamidine • oral clindamycin and primaquine • oral atovaquone • oral trimethoprim and dapsone • nebulised pentamidine is occasionally suggested for mild to moderate infection but is now generally reserved for prophylax- is. • intravenous trimetrexate plus folinic acid may be a further op- tion to intravenous co-trimoxazole or pentamidine in patients with moderate to severe disease. Adjunctive folinic acid with co-trimoxazole has been asso- ciated with an increased risk of therapeutic failure and death in AIDS patients.5 Combination therapy with co-tri- moxazole and pentamidine is not more effective and is po- tentially more toxic than either drug alone.6 Adjunctive treatment with glucocorticosteroids should be given to patients with severe infection1,2 if they are hypox- ic, and treatment should be started as soon as antimicrobial treatment is begun. Primary prophylaxis is indicated for all HIV-positive ad- olescents and adults (including pregnant women and pa- tients on highly active antiretroviral therapy) with CD4+ T lymphocyte counts lower than 200 cells/microlitre, or a history of oropharyngeal candidiasis.2,7 Infants are at in- creased risk to PCP during their first year of life and, in infants and young children, PCP may occur at higher CD4+ T lymphocyte counts compared with adults. The WHO/UNAIDS/UNICEF8 and US guidelines7 recom- mend that infants under 18 months born to HIV-positive mothers should be given prophylaxis beginning at 4 to 6 weeks of age. Therapy should continue until breast feeding is stopped and the infant is confirmed to be HIV-negative, or for at least 1 year initially. Infants subsequently con- firmed to be HIV-positive should remain on prophylactic therapy. In Europe, some clinicians have tended to have a less aggressive approach and only offer prophylaxis once HIV infection is confirmed or opportunistic infections oc- cur.9 Recommendations for primary prophylaxis in pa- tients without HIV infection suggest that prophylaxis should be considered for patients with primary immune deficiency, severe protein malnutrition, organ or stem cell transplants, persistent CD4+ T lymphocyte counts lower than 200 cells/microlitre, or patients receiving cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapy.2,10,11 Secondary prophylaxis is given to all patients following successful treatment of PCP.2 For both primary and secondary prophylaxis1,4,7 the drug of choice is: • co-trimoxazole Alternative prophylactic regimens1,2,4,7 for patients not able to receive co-trimoxazole are: • dapsone (alone or with pyrimethamine) • aerosolised pentamidine • atovaquone
